questions.text: What does Rust's ownership system describe?

answers.text: Rules that determine who owns values and when their resources are released
A garbage-collection algorithm that periodically scans the heap
Only the rules for choosing stack versus heap storage for local variables
Reference counting that is automatically applied to every value

questions.explanation: Ownership is a set of compiler-checked rules about value owners, moves, and when values are dropped.

questions.text: When are the rules of the ownership system checked?

answers.text: Only after the program starts
By the compiler at compile time
By a garbage collector once per minute
Only by the `cargo test` command

questions.explanation: Ownership rules are checked by the compiler; if they are violated, the program does not compile.

questions.text: From what point is a variable `s` valid within its scope?

answers.text: From the point of declaration
From the start of the file
Only after the first `println!`
Only after leaving the block

questions.explanation: A variable becomes valid when it is declared and remains valid until the end of its scope.

questions.text: Which property of `String` makes it a useful type for understanding ownership?

answers.text: A `String` owns a heap buffer that must be released exactly once
A `String` always stores all of its characters directly on the stack
A `String` does not participate in moves because it implements `Copy`
A `String` uses garbage collection instead of `Drop`

questions.explanation: A `String` has an owning handle and a heap buffer; ownership rules prevent double frees and use-after-move.

questions.text: Why does a mutable, growable `String` need heap memory?

answers.text: Its content size may be unknown at compile time and may change at runtime
Because only strings can use the heap
Because the stack cannot store pointers
Because `String` always has zero size

questions.explanation: Memory for text whose size is unknown or can change is requested from the heap at runtime.

questions.text: When does Rust automatically return a `String`'s memory to the allocator?

answers.text: When the owning variable goes out of scope
Immediately after `String::from`
Only after a manual `free`
After every read of the string

questions.explanation: The memory is released when its owner goes out of scope.

questions.text: What happens after `let x = 5; let y = x;`?

answers.text: Both `x` and `y` remain available and equal 5
`x` always becomes invalid
A double free occurs
The code requires `clone()`

questions.explanation: Integers have a fixed size and are trivially copied, so both variables remain valid.

questions.text: What happens after `let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1;`?

answers.text: Ownership moves to `s2`, and `s1` can no longer be used
The heap data is automatically deeply copied
`s2` becomes `&String`
Both variables receive independent data without any extra operation

questions.explanation: For `String`, this is a move: `s1` becomes invalid and `s2` remains valid.

questions.text: How do you explicitly create a deep copy of a `String`'s data?

answers.text: Call `clone()`
Use ordinary assignment
Add `mut`
Call `drop()`

questions.explanation: `clone()` is used for an explicit deep copy of heap data.

questions.text: What does implementing the `Copy` trait mean for assignment?

answers.text: The value is trivially copied and the original variable remains valid
The value is always moved
`clone()` is always called
The data must be allocated on the heap

questions.explanation: For `Copy` types, assignment does not invalidate the original variable.

questions.text: Which restriction relates `Copy` and `Drop`?

answers.text: Rust does not allow `Copy` if the type or one of its parts implements `Drop`
Every `Drop` implementation automatically implies `Copy`
`Copy` is allowed only for `String`
There is no restriction between them

questions.explanation: The material explicitly states that a type with `Drop` cannot also be annotated as `Copy`.

questions.text: How can a function's return value affect ownership?

answers.text: It can transfer ownership to the calling code
It never affects ownership
It always returns only a reference
It is automatically cloned regardless of type

questions.explanation: The chapter shows that return values can also transfer ownership.

questions.text: Which statements are Rust ownership rules? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Every value has an owner
At any moment, a value has only one owner
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped
Every value must have two owners

questions.explanation: These are the three basic ownership rules stated at the start of Chapter 4.

questions.text: Which statements about the stack are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It follows LIFO order
Stored data must have a known fixed size
Pushing and popping happen at the top of the stack
The stack requires the operating system to search for an arbitrary free region

questions.explanation: The stack is sequential, follows LIFO order, and does not require a search for free space like the heap does.

questions.text: What is typically placed on the stack when a function is called? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Values passed to the function
The function's local variables
Possible pointers to heap data
The entire operating system

questions.explanation: When a function is called, its passed values and local variables are placed on the stack; they are removed when the function finishes.

questions.text: Which statements about the scope of variable `s` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Before declaration, `s` is invalid
After declaration, `s` is valid
After the scope closes, `s` is invalid
`s` is always available throughout the file regardless of blocks

questions.explanation: Listing 4-1 shows the period during which a variable is valid inside its scope.

questions.text: Which operations are valid for a mutable `String`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Create it with `String::from`
Append text with `push_str`
Declare the variable with `mut` so it can be changed
Modify a string literal directly without `String`

questions.explanation: The example uses `let mut s = String::from(...)` and `s.push_str(...)`.

questions.text: Which requirements for managing `String` memory are described? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Request memory at runtime
Return the memory when the `String` is no longer needed
Correctly pair allocation and deallocation
A garbage collector must be used

questions.explanation: The chapter explains the need to allocate and return memory and how Rust automates the latter through ownership.

questions.text: Which statements about `drop` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Rust calls it automatically when the owner goes out of scope
A type's implementation can use it to release memory
In the example it is associated with the closing brace of the scope
The user must manually write `drop` for every `String` at the end of each block

questions.explanation: `drop` is invoked automatically; a manual call at every use site is not required.

questions.text: Which parts of a `String` value are stored on the stack? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Pointer
Length
Capacity
The bytes of the contents `hello`

questions.explanation: The string bytes are on the heap, while the pointer, length, and capacity form the stack representation.

questions.text: Which statements about `String` length and capacity are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Length is the amount of memory in bytes currently used by the contents
Capacity is the total amount of memory obtained from the allocator
Both values are part of the `String` stack representation
Capacity is always zero for a nonempty string

questions.explanation: The figure and text define `len` and `capacity` in exactly this way.

questions.text: Which actions occur for `let s2 = s1;` with a `String`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The pointer is copied
The length is copied
The capacity is copied
The heap data is automatically deeply copied

questions.explanation: The stack fields are copied, while the heap data is not duplicated automatically.

questions.text: Why does Rust make `s1` invalid after a move? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: To avoid two owners of the same heap memory
To prevent double free
To preserve memory safety
To force every `String` to live only on the stack

questions.explanation: Invalidating the old variable prevents double free and preserves the single-owner rule.

questions.text: Which statements about `clone()` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It creates a deep copy of a `String`'s heap data
It explicitly signals a potentially expensive operation
After cloning, both strings can be used
It is identical to an ordinary move with no heap copy

questions.explanation: `clone` is an explicit deep copy and a visible, potentially expensive operation in the code.

questions.text: Which types commonly implement `Copy`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Integer types
`bool`
Floating-point types
`String`

questions.explanation: The list also includes `char` and tuples made only of `Copy` types; `String` is not included.

questions.text: Which of these tuples can implement `Copy`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A tuple containing only `Copy` types
`(bool, char)`
`(i32, String)`

questions.explanation: A tuple implements `Copy` only if all of its elements implement `Copy`; `String` does not satisfy that condition.

questions.text: Which statements about passing values to functions are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The mechanics are analogous to assignment
A `String` can be moved into a parameter
An `i32` can be copied when passed
Passing to a function always creates a deep clone for every type

questions.explanation: Function calls follow the same move/copy rules as assignment.

questions.text: Suppose a function takes a parameter `s: String`. What happens when `consume(s)` is called? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Unless `s` was cloned beforehand, ownership of the `String` moves into the function parameter
After the call, the original variable `s` can no longer be used as the owner of that value
If the function neither moves the value onward nor returns it, the `String` is dropped when the parameter leaves scope
The compiler automatically performs a deep `clone()` before every such call

questions.explanation: Passing a `String` by value moves ownership. The owner inside the function is responsible for dropping it unless ownership is moved again.

questions.text: What consequences does `Copy` have when an `i32` value is passed to a function by value? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The function receives a separate copy of the value
The original variable remains usable after the call
No explicit call to `clone()` is required for this copy
The original variable becomes invalid just like a `String` after a move

questions.explanation: `i32` implements `Copy`: copying is implicit, so passing the argument does not invalidate the original variable.

questions.text: Which statements about cleaning up heap data when leaving scope are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The current valid owner performs the cleanup
If data was moved, the old variable has nothing to free
`drop` is called for the owner when it leaves scope
After a move, both variables must free the same memory

questions.explanation: After a move, the new owner is the only valid owner and is responsible for releasing the data.

questions.text: Why is passing a `String` by value merely to read its length usually less convenient than borrowing it? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The function takes ownership even though it only needs read access
For the caller to keep owning the same string, ownership would have to be returned or otherwise transferred back
A reference lets the function compute the length without taking ownership
Borrowing requires a deep copy of the string buffer

questions.explanation: Borrowing lets a function read a `String` without a move and without returning ownership to the caller.
